This cruiser is marked with the Boston Police Logo and Is equipped with functioning blue and white lights and sirens. The officer observed MA Registration XXX#1, a gray 2010s Honda or Acura four-door sedan traveling on Norfolk Street just before Capen Street toward Talbot Avenue. The officer was traveling the opposite direction of Vehicle #1 and observed the motor vehicle to have no front plate displayed (MGL c90 s6) and excessive window tint on the front windshield (MGL c90 s9D). The window tint of Vehicle #1 was so dark the officer could neither ascertain an age, race, or gender of the operator nor number of other possible occupants. The officer conducted a U-turn in the area of Crowell Street and observed that Vehicle #1 had a tinted license plate cover obscuring the rear license plate (MGL c90 s6). The officer also observed the motor vehicle had a black rear bumper which was a different color than the rest of the motor vehicle. The officer followed Vehicle #1 on Norfolk Street and conducted an inquiry of the rear license plate on the Criminal Justice Information System (CJIS) which did not yield any results (MGL c90 s9). The officer attempted to conduct a traffic stop of Vehicle #1 by activating the cruisers blue lights and sirens as Vehicle #1 took a right-hand turn off of Norfolk Street onto Chipman Street. Vehicle #1 failed to stop for the officer (MGL c90 s25) on Chipman Street, and instead increased its speed as it took a right-hand turn onto Torrey Street failing to stop for the marked stop sign (MGL c89 s9). Vehicle #1 proceeded to take another right-hand turn onto Wentworth Street, failing to stop for the marked stop sign (MGL c89 s9). The officer called off the motor vehicle’s current location, the motor vehicle’s registration, the reason for the stop, and direction of flight over Boston Police Radio channel 3. Vehicle #1 continued to evade the officer by traveling down Wentworth Street and taking a left back onto Norfolk Street. The officer pursued Vehicle #1 and observed the motor vehicle cross the double yellow line dividing the two lanes of travel on Norfolk Street (MGL c89 s4A) and fail to stop for the solid red light (MGL c89 s9) at the intersection of Norfolk Street and Woodrow Avenue. The motor vehicle was weaving between lanes and traveling at a high rate of speed at this time (MGL c90 s24). The C907 (Sergeant Bissonnette) called off the motor vehicle pursuit. Officers in the area last observed Vehicle #1 at the intersection of River Street and Central Avenue traveling into the town of Milton. The officers gave the motor vehicle plate, description, and flight to Boston Police Operations to provide to Milton over the Boston Area Police Emergency Radio Network (BAPERN).

Sergeant Dunn had a print out of the City of Boston's Ordinance Manual pages 56-62 which refers to noise pollution, arrest and seizures. Sergeant Dunn approached the group and clearly articulated that the group was violating City Ordnance 16-26, which states: 1. Noise measured in excess of 50dBa between the hours of 11:00 p.m. and 7:00 a.m., or in excess of 70dBa at all other hours 2. In the absence of an applicable noise level standard or regulation of the Air Pollution Control Commission, any noise plainly audible at a distance of three hundred (300”) feet or, in the case of loud amplification devices or similar equipment, noise plainly audible at a distance of one hundred (100’) feet from its source by a person of normal hearing. Sergeant Dunn used the BPD Academy recommended app "dB Meter" to show the group that their audible decimal level was consistently about the 70 db requirement. Sergeant Dunn also showed the group the print out of the Ordinance Manual. Sergeant Dunn stated that if they continued to ignore the officers request they would be subject to arrest, which is consistent with MGL Ch. 272 S. 59: "Provides a police office with the right of arrest for any violation of a city ordinance, rule or regulation, which occurs in his presence" "The words "whoever remains in willful violations", implies that a warning must be given and ignored by the violator before an arrest can be made under MGL c 272 s 59" After being informed of their violation, the protesters stopped using their amplification devices. It should be noted that both the rear left and rear right turn signal functioned properly at this time, indicating that the operator chose NOT to use them during his previous, rapid, unsafe lane changes. The Taxi only stopped as traffic ahead of it was stopped at the red light where the Bowker Overpass intersects with Boylston Street. At this point, Det. At this time, the Subject laid straight back, and extended his legs forward while presenting what could have been signs of a seizure. Persons in the unruly crowd that had gathered and were filming the interaction began yelling that the Subject has a history of seizures. At this time dispatch was advised and an ambulance requested for the Subject/Prisoner. While awaiting the ambulance arrival, the Officer and Trooper did place the Subject into the recovery position on his left side, while a court officer stayed by the Subject's head, placing his hands underneath it to prevent any injury against the ground should he convulse again. The Officers did reassure the Subject that EMS was on the way. During this time, the Subject never lost consciousness, did not foam at the mouth, and his chest and belly were observed continually rising and falling in the same manner while the Subject breathed in and out uninterrupted. Officer Diaz did pull back the Subject's furry hood on his winter coat, and pulled down the "sheisty" ski mask that was covering his face, in order to provide an even more clear airway for him. Moments later, BFD Ladder04 and Boston EMS Ambulance 2A02 (Koo/Sullivan) responded. The Subject was placed on the stretcher and the handcuffs were repositioned to the side rails, one on each wrist. At about 7:11 p.m. on Tuesday, September 2, 2025, while working the front desk at Boston Police Department District D-14 (Brighton/ Allston neighborhoods) XXXWashington Street, Brighton Officer Coleman was approached by an unknown male individual who requested assistance in locating his 78-year-old father. The male reported that his father had been gone for approximately two hours while driving his Subaru to pick up an unknown party. The male further stated that his father did not have his cellular phone with him. The individual expressed interest in having Boston Police compel Subaru to provide the real-time GPS coordinates of the vehicle. The unknown individual indicated concern for his father’s location, but emphasized law enforcement obtaining GPS data over filing a missing person’s report. Officer Coleman conferred with Sgt. Murphy, who directed him to the Detectives Unit. Officer Coleman, then, spoke with Detective O’Connor, who advised Officer Coleman there was not sufficient legal basis for law enforcement to compel Subaru to provide GPS coordinates. Additionally, Officer Coleman consulted with Sgt. Det. Martin Joseph regarding the matter who requested this report to be completed. Officer Coleman returned to inform the individual that if he was genuinely concerned for his father’s safety, the appropriate step would be to contact 911 and request that an officer respond to the residence where his father was last seen, in accordance with Rule 317 and Department practice: the initial responding officer should be dispatched to, or respond to, the location where the missing person was last observed. The individual stated that he believed his father was “probably lost, not missing,” and reiterated his interest in law enforcement forcing Subaru to disclose GPS data. I advised him that GPS tracking is considered a search under United States v. Jones, 565 U.S. 400 (2012) and Carpenter v. United States, 585 U.S. ___ (2018), and that compelling Subaru to release such data without a warrant or court order would constitute a violation of the Fourth Amendment. I explained that lawful process supported by probable cause is required and that the circumstances presented his father not carrying his phone did not rise to the level of exigency. The individual then inquired what would happen if he reported the vehicle stolen. I advised him that filing a false report of a crime for the purpose of obtaining GPS data would constitute a violation of M.G.L. c. 268, § 39 and could result in criminal charges. Officer Coleman further advised the unknown individual of alternative lawful options, including the availability of aftermarket GPS tracking devices. Officer Coleman advised unknown individual to reconsider the limitations of subscribing to a GPS service that does not provide immediate consumer access. The individual was provided with the contact number for the Boston Police Dispatch Call Center +1 (617) 343-4911 should he change his mind and wish to file a missing person’s report. The unknown individual had not called to file a missing person report since this report was completed at the end of Officer Coleman's shift.
